objective: Provide crisis intervention and stabilize a client in acute distress
secondaryObjectives: Advocate for needed services, build service networks and plan discharge, aftercare and wraparound follow-up

brief.situation: You are a clinical social worker at a community mental health agency's walk-in crisis hour. Marisol Vega, 38 (a fictional client), comes in at nine. A fire destroyed her apartment building last night; she and her two children, 7 and 11, got out. The children are at her cousin's. She has a plastic bag of papers and the clothes she slept in. You have an hour.
handover: No prior contact with the agency. Intake has her name and phone number only.
The agency keeps emergency funds, bus passes and a list of local disaster-relief and housing contacts.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Marisol answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 60 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.note: The agency's walk-in crisis slot is an hour; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended start: 'I'm glad you came in. What's happening right now?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "Everything's gone. Everything. The kids are at my cousin's but she's only got one room. I don't know where we sleep tonight. I can't think."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Marisol nods, eyes wet. "Yeah. I just keep shaking."

ground.label: Slow down with her: water, a seat, slow breaths together, and noticing she is safe in this room right now

effects.log: You bring her water, slow your own breathing, and help her notice the room.

then.finding: She drinks. Her shoulders come down a little. "Okay. I'm here."

askLethality.label: Ask directly, as part of the assessment, about thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone, and about the children's safety now

effects.log: You ask directly about thoughts of suicide or harming anyone, without asking for details, and where the children are.

then.finding: "No. God, no. I have to be okay for them. They're safe at Rosa's, her husband's home."
"Why are you asking me that?" (She does not answer.)

effects.log: Crisis intervention begins with a lethality and safety assessment (Roberts, stage 1).

listProblems.label: Help her sort the most urgent problems: where to sleep tonight, clothes and food, the children's school, documents
listProblems.available: not talking and (grounded and not problemsListed)
listProblems.why: Help her settle a little first.

effects.log: You help her list what is urgent, in order.

effects.finding: "Tonight is the big one. Then clothes. The kids have school Monday. My ID was in my wallet, and the wallet's gone."

hearFeelings.label: Make room for what she feels: the fear last night, the loss, being the one who has to hold it together
hearFeelings.available: not talking and (grounded and not feelingsHeard)
hearFeelings.why: Help her settle a little first.

effects.log: You invite and reflect her feelings, briefly and simply.

effects.finding: "I carried my son down the stairs. I keep smelling it." She cries, then wipes her face. "I can't fall apart. They need me."

exploreOptions.label: Explore options with her: her cousin for a night or two, the disaster-relief lodging line, the agency's emergency fund, her employer
exploreOptions.available: not talking and (problemsListed and not optionsExplored)

effects.log: You explore the options with her and ask what she prefers.

effects.finding: "Rosa will do two nights if I ask. After that a motel, if the relief line covers it. I'll call work myself."

makeCalls.label: Make the first calls with her, with her consent: the disaster-relief lodging line and the school, her on the phone, you beside her
makeCalls.available: not talking and (optionsExplored and not callsMade)

effects.log: You make the calls together, Marisol speaking and you helping.

effects.finding: The relief line books two weeks of lodging starting Saturday. The school will hold the children's places and has clothes in the family closet.

effects.log: Advocacy and linking to services, with her doing as much as she can (Roberts, stages 5 and 6).

plan.label: Write the next 48 hours down with her: tonight at Rosa's, Saturday's lodging, clothes from the school, ID replacement, emergency fund for food
plan.available: not talking and (optionsExplored and not actionPlan)

effects.log: You write the plan with her, in her words.

effects.finding: She reads it back. "Rosa's tonight. Motel Saturday. Clothes Monday at school. ID Tuesday. That I can do."

followUp.label: Set a follow-up: you call her tomorrow, and an appointment this week for her and the children

effects.log: You set a call for tomorrow and an appointment this week.

effects.finding: "Tomorrow, after ten. And the kids, yes. My daughter won't stop asking if it'll happen again."

forms.label: Start with the agency's full intake: history, insurance, household, mental health history

effects.log: You begin the full intake form.

effects.finding: She stares at the clipboard. "I don't know my insurance number. It burned."

effects.log: In acute crisis, assessment is brief and focused; a full intake now delays stabilization.

listOnlyA.label: Give her the resource list and tell her to call the numbers when she can

effects.log: You hand her the list.

effects.finding: She holds it without reading it. "Okay."

effects.log: A list handed to someone who 'can't think' is not crisis intervention; link her, with her, to the help.

probeTrauma.label: Ask her to describe the night of the fire in detail, from the start

effects.log: You ask for a detailed account of the fire.

effects.finding: She starts, then stops, shaking again. "The smoke. I can't."

takeOver.label: Tell her you will handle everything and make all the decisions for her today

effects.log: You tell her you will take care of it all.
Doing everything for her undercuts her own coping; crisis work restores her capacity to act (NASW 1.02).

promise.label: Promise her that she will have a new apartment within the week

effects.log: You promise a new apartment within the week.
You close the session.

options.label: Stabilized: oriented, distress down, no thoughts of suicide or harm, children safe, a written 48-hour plan
A call tomorrow; an appointment this week for her and the children

effects.log: Documented: {stateDoc}, follow-up {followDoc}.

source.note: Each exchange costs the minutes a real exchange of that kind takes, rounded to whole minutes.

effects.log: The 60-minute hour is up. The session ends here.
Marisol stands, says she has to go find somewhere for her kids, and leaves before the hour is over.

first.title: Predict (not scored)
first.context: Marisol is shaking and says she can't think. Before anything else: where does crisis intervention start?

choices.label: Calm and orient her, and assess safety and lethality; then the problems, feelings, options and a plan

effects.log: Prediction: stabilize and assess first.

choices.feedback: Right. Roberts' model starts with a lethality and safety assessment and rapport, then the major problems, feelings, alternatives, an action plan and follow-up; Psychological First Aid puts safety, comfort and stabilization first.

choices.label: A full intake, so you have the whole picture

effects.log: Prediction: full intake.

choices.feedback: Not in acute crisis. Assessment is brief and focused on safety and the immediate problems; the full intake can wait.

choices.label: Resources: she needs housing, so give her the numbers

effects.log: Prediction: resources first.

choices.feedback: She needs them, but she cannot use a list while she cannot think. Stabilize, then link her to help with her.

formulation.question: Write your formulation: how you stabilized Marisol, what you assessed, and the plan and follow-up she left with.

parts.label: Stabilizing and assessing
parts.criteria: Grounded first (water, breathing, orientation); a direct lethality and safety question (none; the children safe); urgent problems sorted; feelings heard briefly; no full intake, no detailed retelling.
parts.modelAnswer: I helped Marisol settle first: water, slow breathing, noticing she is safe in the room. I asked directly about thoughts of suicide or harming anyone (none) and where the children are (safe with her cousin). We sorted what is urgent: a bed tonight, clothes, school, her ID. I made room for her feelings briefly; I did not ask her to retell the fire or start a full intake.

parts.label: Plan and follow-up
parts.criteria: Options explored with her; calls made together, with her consent and her doing what she can; a written 48-hour plan; a call tomorrow and an appointment for her and the children; no promises you cannot keep, no taking over.
parts.modelAnswer: We explored the options and she chose: Rosa's for two nights, then the relief line's lodging. We called the relief line and the school together, with her speaking. The plan for the next 48 hours is written in her words. I will call her tomorrow, and she and the children have an appointment this week.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Not used by this case's endings: stabilization is judged by her state at the close and the plan.

noProgress.rationale: A family without a bed tonight, and no plan made with her: the crisis is untouched.

expertPath.text: Ground her: water, slow breathing, orientation; ask directly about suicide and harm, and where the children are.
Sort the urgent problems with her; make room for what she feels.
Explore options; make the lodging and school calls together; write the 48-hour plan.
A call tomorrow and an appointment for her and the children; document.

stabilized.headline: Good: crisis intervention, stage by stage
stabilized.body: You stabilized first, assessed lethality and the children's safety, sorted the problems, heard her, and linked her to help with her in charge, then set follow-up (Roberts; Psychological First Aid).

gaps.headline: Stabilized, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria below show what was missing.

walkout.headline: She left
walkout.body: A full intake, a request to retell the fire, or a handed-over list can push a person in crisis back out the door.

noPlan.headline: Sent off with a list
noPlan.body: In acute crisis, a person often cannot act on information alone. Link her to the help, with her, and write the plan down.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Crisis intervention starts with stabilization and a brief, focused assessment: ground her (water, breathing, orientation) and ask directly about suicide and harm to others and where the children are (Roberts, stage 1; Psychological First Aid). Then sort the urgent problems with her, make brief room for her feelings, explore options and let her choose, and link her to help by making calls together rather than handing over a list or taking over. Write a 48-hour plan in her words and set follow-up: a call tomorrow and an appointment for her and the children. Avoid a full intake now, a detailed retelling of the fire, and promises you cannot keep.
